newsitem.title: USA: Atlanta Fed's Guynn sees U.S. '97 GDP at 2-2.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Atlanta Fed's Guynn sees U.S. '97 GDP at 2-2.5 pct.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Jack Guynn said on Monday he expects the U.S. Gross Domestic Product to expand in 1997 at a healthy rate of between 2.0 percent and 2.50 percent while the inflation rate would remain little changed at around 3.0 percent.
"We're coming off a year in which the economy performed very well. I believe we're going to see more of the same in 1997," Guynn told the Atlanta Rotary Club.

"It looks like another year of moderate growth somewhere between 2.0 percent and 2.5 percent, unemployment continuing near the low level of 5.5 percent... and inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, continuing at about its current 3.0-percent level," Guynn forecast.
The Atlanta Fed president, who votes at the Federal Open Market Committee in 1997, predicted "consumers will be leading the way, though not quite as vigorously as last year."
Guynn also expected business spending to further contribute to economic growth in 1997, while the impact of government spending and trade would be similar to 1996.

Turning to the dangers the U.S. economy may face this year, Guynn cited "continued tightness in labor markets... a real concern for business people and policymakers," because this risks to push inflation higher.
"Labor markets are at least a question mark in my mind," the Atlanta Fed president said.
Other dangers included "growing levels of consumer indebtedness" and "real estate ... overbuilding."
Guynn emphasized the role played by the 19-member U.S. policymakers.
"FOMC meetings are not a rubber-stamping session for (Fed Chairman) Alan Greenspan. There are a lot of people sitting at the table debating and making the decisions," Guynn stressed.

"Actually, there are 19 of us who sit around the FOMC table and debate the state of the economy amd monetary policy," Guynn further pointed out. "We all participate fully in the discussion, whether we're voting members or not."
Guynn hinted at what his own vote will be in the Fed's anti-inflation fight.
"I would prefer to see inflation somewhat lower than somewhat higher," Guynn stated, while spelling out the pivotal issue in U.S. monetary policy at the moment.
"If we want to maintain the current rate of inflation, then the Fed's current stance is probably appropriate under current conditions," Guynn acknowledged.
"If we want to make further progress on inflation, then we need to be looking for opportunities over time to nudge the rate still lower," the Atlanta Fed president added.
Guynn, however, conceded he is "not a zealot who wants to take a sort of 'damn the torpedoes' approach to achieve a goal of zero inflation no matter what."

Turning to fiscal issues, Guynn cautioned "the deficit problem in some ways is worse than current numbers indicate," in part because "the Social Security Trust Fund is projected to go from a surplus that is being used to offset the federal deficit to insolvency over the next generation."
